title: God in the dust of the road
hookLine: a poet tells a worshiper to open the temple doors and look outside
carry: seva: god is with the ones who work

cards: A dark corner of a temple. The doors are shut. Someone sits there with a string of beads, chanting, eyes closed.
It's a real and honored form of devotion. And in one Gitanjali poem, the poet walks up to that person and says, in effect: stop. Open your eyes.
Your God isn't before you. Today, poem eleven, and where Tagore says to look instead.

teach.h: LEAVE THE CHANTING, OPEN YOUR EYES.
teach.b: Here are the opening lines, in Tagore's own English: "Leave this chanting and singing and telling of beads! Whom dost thou worship in this lonely dark corner of a temple with doors all shut? Open thine eyes and see thy God is not before thee!"

teach.h: GOD IS WITH THE TILLER AND THE PATHMAKER.
teach.b: Then he says where God is: "He is there where the tiller is tilling the hard ground and where the pathmaker is breaking stones."
God is with them in sun and in shower, the poem says, his garment covered in dust, and it tells the worshiper to put off the holy mantle and come down onto the dusty soil too.
Tagore's family belonged to the Brahmo Samaj, a reform movement wary of image worship, and the poem carries that voice.
Hindus who pray with beads and flowers may answer that their worship is where they learn to see God in the field. But both stand on one old teaching.

teach.h: THE LORD DWELLS IN EVERY HEART.
teach.b: In the Gita, Krishna says the Lord dwells in the heart of every being. If that's true, God isn't only behind the shut doors.
The poem even asks where deliverance could be found, since the master himself has joyfully taken on the bonds of creation.
Hindus have a word for worship done with the hands: seva, service.
Temple kitchens run on it, volunteers chopping and stirring so anyone who walks in can eat, and many families count that hour as worship, not time away from it.
The poem closes: meet him and stand by him in toil and in the sweat of thy brow. The place of worship and the place of work turn out to be the same place.

how: Many Hindu temples run kitchens where volunteers cook and serve whoever comes, and many families count this seva as worship alongside prayer with beads, flowers and incense.

o: Tagore's songs, finding God in the dust of people's work
Tagore's call to leave all work and live as a hermit
a temple manual for chanting with a string of beads

games.q: Gitanjali, poem eleven — tap the pairs.
p: a temple with doors all shut

s: poem eleven objects only to the shut doors, not to the beads
it says plainly: leave this chanting and singing and telling of beads, and come out into the dust.
the poem says God's garment is covered in dust
he is with the workers in sun and in shower.
the poem promises deliverance from the world
it asks where deliverance could be found, since the master himself has taken on the bonds of creation.

games.q: Nani asks you to skip the puja hall and help in the temple kitchen. by Tagore's poem, are you missing God?
o: yes. God is only in the shrine.
no. God is with the ones who work, and seva is worship too.
it doesn't matter. God isn't anywhere.
games.why: Tagore finds God where the tiller tills and the pathmaker breaks stones, and Hindus call worship done with the hands seva. the shrine and the kitchen both count.

practice: Open your eyes and let your gaze rest on what's in front of you.
Bring to mind someone whose work you depend on and rarely see, whoever grew today's food, laid the road outside or cleans the building, and stay with one of them, at work in sun or rain.
If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer, right where they're working; if not, simply keep them in view, with some gratitude.

wordCard.voice: Tagore's Gitanjali. In poem eleven, the doors come open, and God is found where the tiller tills and the pathmaker breaks stones.
